query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding TC4 with a Ni-modified refractory high-entropy alloy coating will significantly enhance surface hardness and wear resistance while maintaining the substrate’s beneficial bulk properties.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloy with an α+β dual-phase microstructure exhibiting low hardness and high wear rates under extreme-service conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply laser cladding of a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) coating that includes Ni (targeting around 6 at.% Ni) onto the TC4 surface.
generation.conditions: The process is executed under controlled laser parameters to achieve rapid cooling, minimize dilution, and ensure strong metallurgical bonding. Testing should be performed under standardized wear load conditions (e.g., 10 N and 30 N) and ambient temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The rapid solidification during laser cladding promotes the formation of fine dendritic microstructures along with a eutectic phase and a solid solution with Ni, which together improve hardness and inhibit crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The incorporation of Ni within the RHEA coating is expected to induce solid solution strengthening and grain refinement. The laser cladding process yields a dense, well-adhered coating by limiting heat input and residual stresses, thereby preserving the substrate’s integrity while significantly enhancing the surface properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: An approximate 50–80% increase in surface hardness and a significant reduction in wear rate (exceeding 60% improvement) compared to untreated TC4, as well as improved resistance to crack initiation and propagation at the coating–substrate interface.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4 alloy known for low hardness and poor wear resistance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized improvements are expected only if the laser cladding parameters effectively control dilution and heat input; significant deviations in Ni content or processing conditions may lead to unwanted intermetallic formation, residual stresses, or poor coating–substrate bonding.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements depend on optimization of the Ni proportion and specific laser cladding parameters; the observed enhancements might vary based on processing precision and environmental conditions during wear testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of TC4 samples: one group will receive the Ni-modified RHEA laser cladding treatment (with varying Ni contents of 0, 3, 6, and 9 at.%) and a control group with untreated TC4. All samples will be processed under identical laser cladding conditions optimized for minimal dilution and adequate bonding. Perform systematic evaluations including microstructural analysis (TEM, XRD), microhardness testing, and reciprocating sliding wear tests under standard loads (10 N and 30 N).
measurements: Wear rate and volume loss measurements under set loads
Microstructural characterizations to assess phase composition and interface quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the laser-cladded samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in hardness and wear resistance compared to untreated TC4, or if detrimental microstructures (such as cracks, excessive intermetallic formation, or poor interface bonding) are consistently identified in the treated samples.

cited_evidence.text: By laser cladding a RHEA coating on the surface of titanium alloy, the advantages of the high strength and plasticity of the titanium alloy can be combined with the corrosion resistance of RHEA, which not only solves the defects of titanium alloy, but also greatly reduces the production cost and consumption in service. At present, there is little research on the corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys composed of refractory metal elements, but their excellent performance cannot be ignored. Jiang [] et al. prepared TiZrAlNb and TiZrAlNbCo high-entropy alloy coatings on the surface of TC4 titanium alloy using laser cladding technology. Through a study of their microstructure and corrosion resistance, it was found that the TiZrAlNb and TiZrAlNbCo high-entropy alloy coatings were, respectively, BCC and BCC-fcc matrix phases, and were accompanied by a small number of intermetallic compounds; the dendritic crystals of the TiZrAlNbCo alloy coating were much finer than those of the TiZrAlNb alloy coating. In this study, the surface of (Ti-6Al-4V)TC4 alloy was modified via laser cladding. The elemental composition of the coating was (TiAl)95−xCu5Nix, with Ni as the variable (where x = 0, 3, 6, and 9 at.%). Multi-principal alloy coatings were successfully prepared, and their constituent phases, microstructures, and chemical compositions were thoroughly investigated. The hardness and wear resistance of the coatings were analyzed, and the compositions and interfacial characteristics of the different phases were examined via transmission electron microscopy. The analysis revealed that Ni formed a solid solution and a eutectic structure in the Ti(Al, Cu)2 phase. These findings provide valuable insights into the coating properties. Moreover, reciprocal dry sliding friction experiments were conducted to investigate the wear mechanism. The results revealed a significant increase in wear resistance owing to the formation of a Ni solid solution and changes in the coating structure. Additionally, tensile tests demonstrated that the tensile strength of the coatings initially increased and then decreased with varying Ni content.
